statement.p: Find the critical point of the function f(x,y)=42x-6y^{2}-\ln\mathopen{}\left(\left|x+y\right|\right).

Use the Second Derivative Test to determine whether it is
a saddle point
test fails
a local minimum
a local maximum

static.solution:
f(x,y)=42x-6y^{2}-\ln\mathopen{}\left(\left|x+y\right|\right) equal to zero and solve f_x(x,y)=42-\frac{1}{x+y}=0 f_y(x,y)=-\left(12y+\frac{1}{x+y}\right)=0 The first equation implies that \frac{1}{x+y}=42. Substituting into the second equation gives -\left(12y+42\right)=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad y=-3.5 We substitute y=-3.5 in the first equation and solve for x: 42-\frac{1}{x - 3.5}=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x - 3.5=\frac{1}{42} \quad \Rightarrow \quad x=\frac{ + 3.5 \cdot 42 + 1}{42}=\frac{148}{42} We obtain critical point \left(\frac{148}{42}, -3.5\right).
Notice, that although f_x and f_y do not exist where x+y=0, these are not critical points, since f is not defined at these points.
Now we compute the Discriminant. We find the second-order partials: f_{xx}(x,y)=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(42-\frac{1}{x+y}\right)=\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}} f_{yy}(x,y)=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(-\left(12y+\frac{1}{x+y}\right)\right)=\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}}-12 f_{xy}(x,y)=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(42-\frac{1}{x+y}\right)=\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}} The discriminant is thus D(x,y)=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2=\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}}-12\right)-\frac{1}{(x+y)^4}=-\frac{12}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}}
Applying the Second Derivative Test we have D\left(\frac{148}{42},-3.5\right)=-21168\lt 0 We conclude that f\left(\frac{148}{42},-3.5\right) is a saddle point.
